books.section: United States Victory in the Spanish-American War

stimulus.source_note: William Dinwiddie, photograph, 1898; Library of Congress LCCN96521936; public domain.
stimulus.text: The photograph shows a large group of soldiers in slouch hats posed on a hilltop in Cuba. Theodore Roosevelt stands at the center in a dark shirt, light trousers, and a slouch hat, his hands on his hips, with an American flag on a pole behind him. A typewritten caption strip at the bottom of the mounted print names the Battle of San Juan and the photographer, William Dinwiddie, 1898.

source: original; stimulus is a public-domain 1898 photograph by William Dinwiddie
stem: The photograph shows Theodore Roosevelt standing at the center of his men on the hill they had just captured. The image is best used to illustrate

options.text: How Roosevelt's wartime service made him a national figure
The navy's victory at Manila Bay
options.misconception: Manila Bay was a naval battle in the Philippines, fought by Dewey's squadron, not by Roosevelt's regiment.

options.text: The signing of the Treaty of Paris
options.misconception: The treaty was signed in Paris in December; this is a battlefield photograph from Cuba in July.

options.text: The Rough Riders' defeat at Santiago de Cuba in July
options.misconception: The photograph shows a victory pose on a captured hill, not a defeat.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Roosevelt's charge up San Juan Hill made headlines and lifted him into national politics.
rationales.B: Manila Bay belonged to Commodore Dewey and the navy, half a world away from Roosevelt's regiment in Cuba.
rationales.C: The treaty was signed in Paris months later. This photograph was taken on a Cuban hilltop in 1898.
rationales.D: The men pose as victors on the hill they captured. Nothing in the image shows a defeat.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the center. Roosevelt stands in the middle of his men, with the flag behind him.
2. Read the caption. The print names the Battle of San Juan, the hill the regiment had just captured.
3. Ask what followed. The books say the charge made Roosevelt a hero and lifted his political standing.
Remember: a photograph of a leader at the center of his men is evidence about reputation, so ask what the reputation bought.

figures.caption: Colonel Roosevelt and his Rough Riders atop the hill they captured, Battle of San Juan, photographed by William Dinwiddie, 1898.
